messages.subject: How to run multiple unmarked models in parallel?
messages.subject_clean: How to run multiple unmarked models in parallel?
messages.body_plain:
Dear friends,

There has been some discussion about using parallel processing to reduce the time required to use parboot() to evaluate goodness-of-fit of a particular unmarked model. For example, here are two threads providing good solutions:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/unmarked/txp1UeptjgM/bYHTPiUN55kJ

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/parallel$20parboot$20%7Csort:date/unmarked/9vXaxj-7chU/jfgX4WEKBAAJ

Now, I'd like to use parallel processing to run reduce the time required to fit dozens of gmultmix() models on large datasets. Each of my ~50 models takes ~30 minutes to fit, and I'd like to fit all of the models for ~6 species or guilds, so fitting these one at a time would take several weeks. Thus, my desire to use parallel processing (on a cloud-based machine with 96 cores).

The parboot() examples linked above involve doing the same thing (a parboot call) many times, but this current problem involves doing many things (fit different models) once each. I can't find any coded examples of using parallel processing to fit multiple models in parallel either in the this Google group or elsewhere (stackoverflow etc), so I'm hoping someone here might be able to point me in the right direction.

Many thanks in advance!

Mark B.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

Here's a rough example that should get you started.

Also, the pre-release version of unmarked on Github has a new C++ backend for gmultmix. In my tests the new backend is 10-15 times faster than the old pure-R version, but it only supports the built in pi functions (removal, double).

#run 2 models in parallel
library(unmarked)
library(parallel)

data(frogs)
pferUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(pfer.bin)

#Add second dataset
pferUMF2 <- pferUMF
siteCovs(pferUMF2) <- data.frame(sitevar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF2)))
obsCovs(pferUMF2) <- data.frame(obsvar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF2) * obsNum(pferUMF2)))

#Set up parallel
nmods <- 2
processors <- detectCores() - 1
cl <- makeCluster(processors)

#function to run unmarked in each core
#could add more arguments to call
run_um <- function(x){
  unmarked::occu(as.formula(x[[1]]),x[[2]])
}

#Sets of arguments for each run (list of lists)
#Could add more arguments here
args <- list(mod1=list(formula='~1 ~1', data=pferUMF),
             mod2=list(formula='~obsvar1 ~1', data=pferUMF2))

#Run in parallel
out <- parLapply(cl=cl,X=args,fun=run_um)

stopCluster(cl)
#Result is list with each element being one model output

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

Assuming you are using a recent version of unmarked, parboot already runs simulations in parallel by default when nsim > 100 (as it is in your case, see ?parboot). On your system, it will do so using 15 of the 16 cores with each running one simulation at time until all 1000 are done. If you want to make sure it is doing so you could run 'top' or similar in a terminal on the AWS instance while it runs and make sure it spawns 15 R processes.

In your second example you are doing batches of 100 simulations at a time on only 10 cores, with the extra overhead of loading the library and running the setup code in parboot() in every core. I'm guessing a combination of the lower number of cores and the extra overhead leads to the extra runtime you are seeing.

Ken

Ken

You have to provide each argument to gmultmix in a separate element of each list. In my original example I had only 'formula' and 'data' arguments because that's all occu() needs, but gmultmix needs three separate formulas and potentially the mixture argument.

I wrote out a (shortened) version of your code that hopefully will be more clear (note I didn't actually run this, but it should work):

library(unmarked)
library(parallel)

processors <- detectCores() - 1
cl <- makeCluster(processors)

# define function to run unmarked in each core
run_um <- function(x){

  #assume mixture is poisson unless specified explicitly
  #if you specify the mixture in every list of arguments below you can remove this part
  if(is.null(x$mixture)){
    x$mixture <- "P"
  }

  unmarked::gmultmix(lambdaformula=as.formula(x$lambdaformula),
                      phiformula=as.formula(x$phiformula),
                      pformula=as.formula(x$pformula),
                      mixture=x$mixture,
                      data=x$data)

}

# Sets of arguments for each run (list of lists)

#Each formula and the mixture argument should be their own list element
#I cut out some models just to save typing
args <- list(fm0=list(lambdaformula='~1', phiformula= '~1', pformula='~1', data=ovenFrame),
              fm1 = list(lambdaformula='~ ufc', phiformula='~ 1', pformula='~ 1', data = ovenFrame),
              fm1nb = list(lambdaformula='~ ufc', phiformula='~ 1', pformula='~ 1', mixture = "NB", data = ovenFrame),
              fm2nb = list(lambdaformula='~ trba', phiformula='~ 1', pformula='~ 1', mixture = "NB", data = ovenFrame)
              )

Hello,

I have tried searching for a solution to this error, but have been unable to find anything.  Hence I am seeking guidance here.

I am using code derived from the ISSJ example using the unmarked distsamp function from section 8.4.3 in Kery and Royle's AHM Vol 1 (2016) in RStudio to analyse elephant dung distance sampled data for Mount Kenya, as a part of my PhD. > fall.modsel$hr.Wet1.LCDBoundSlopeDEMWet1 <- distsamp(~pr_Wet1_gg ~LCCode + DistBound + MK_slope_r + MKL10mBuff + pr_Wet1_gg,

  invalid to use names()<- on an S4 object of class 'unmarkedModSel'

Therefore I have been recreating 'fall.modsel' as an empty list and starting again, losing all the models I have already fitted.

Is this something to do with the length of the names I am using for the models?  Or something else?

I can provide further code if needed...

Any help much appreciated.

With thanks in advance,

Gwili

messages.subject_clean: version 2.2.1 of AICcmodavg package now on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The new version (2.2.1) of the AICcmodavg package is now on CRAN. You'll find below a summary of the changes and new functionalities potentially of interest to unmarked users.

Major changes:

- new function 'summaryOD' to compute confidence intervals around estimates (out.type = "confint") or hypothesis tests (out.type = "nhst") adjusted for overdispersion on models using the Poisson or binomial distributions (xtable method created to output to LaTeX).

- new function 'anovaOD' to compute likelihood ratio tests corrected for overdispersion between two models of various classes that use the Poisson or binomial distributions (xtable method created to output to LaTeX).

- package now supports multispecies occupancy data and models of classes 'unmarkedFrameOccuMulti' and 'unmarkedFitOccuMulti' (for all functions except modavgPred)

- package now fully supports the false positive occupancy models, including the "b" parameter for certain detections

- there is now a 'parallel' argument in 'Nmix.gof.test' and 'mb.gof.test' to control the 'parallel' argument in 'parboot'

- 'mb.chisq' and 'mb.gof.test' now support Royle-Nichols models fit with 'occuRN' (thanks to Dan Linden)

- new functions 'ictab' and 'modavgIC' to do model selection or multimodel inference for information criteria other than AIC, AICc, QAIC, or QAICc. This requires the user to supply a vector of information criteria (e.g., WAIC, DIC).

Minor changes:

- modified default printing of NA to "." for nicer display in 'detHist', 'countDist', 'mb.chisq', with 'xtable'

- modified 'xtable' for nicer printing of K for 'aictab', 'bictab', and 'anovaOD'

Sincerely,

Marc

I don't think you are doing anything wrong, but perhaps there is something wrong with the data ? Occupancy models are in essence a sort of logistic regression models. There is an issue in logistc regression called 'complete separation' (Gelman and Hill book has a section on this, surely also elsewhere). This is when there is strictly no overlap between covariates values for cases with a 0 response and those with a 1 response. In this case, the slope estimate is infinity (I think) and computations break down. Gelman shows that this can be mitigated with just a little bit of additional information provided in the prior of a Bayesian analysis of such a model. We have noted cases of probable complete separation in the application of a dynamic occupancy model (Kery et al., JBiog, 2013), where the predictions of occupancy from some complex models were essentially binary (i.e., either very close to 0 or very close to 1). We then simplified the model and the problem went away.

I don't know whether this is really the case in your example. How does the model fit summary look like for one of your models ? Does the problem appear also when you fit very simple models (e.g., with only a single covariate).

Best regards  --- Marc

Even if you only have typically 2 visits per site, that results in a minimum of 0.98 (= 1- (1-0.86)^2) probability of at least one detection per site.  Therefore, you could likely get away with just performing logistic regression.  And packages that perform logistic regression will likely give you informative warnings or error messages if you have complete separation.

The huge standard errors compared to the estimates of all of the occupancy parameters is also an indication that something is not quite right.

Jim

For whatever it's worth here are my two cents:

1.  As others have said for many situations ignoring the correlation structure doesn't bias estimates.  (xbar is still a good estimate of the mean even if observations are serially correlated - assuming one has enough observations).
2.  However, ignoring correlation structure does have a big effect on estimates of precision.  (My soapbox speech is "A statistic without an appropriate measure of precision is at best of unknown value.")
3.  Maybe it was mentioned in the previous threads (and if so I apologize for missing it) but why not perform a bootstrap to estimate precision of any particular quantity where site is the basic unit of a bootstrap selection?  That would attempt to include the inherent correlation/dependence structure (i.e., all years/seasons for any site would always be included in a bootstrap sample) and result in justifiable estimates of precision.

Jim

Hi Dan and Jim,

interesting discussion. I tend to feel like Dan that I wouldn't see underestimated precision as a death-blow for "stacking". After all, I would say that in almost ANY statistical analysis that we run, we always ignore at least half a dozen dependencies (in time, space etc), which always will cause our SEs to be too narrow.

On the other hand, I find Jim's suggested solution, nonparametric bootstrapping, excellent and it should be easy to enough to implement in R.

Not sure I agree with Jim here.  Ignoring correlation can have an effect on precision, but it does not have to be "big".  Underestimating uncertainty is not necessarily a fatal flaw.

One of the points of stacking sites/years is that there is value in knowing that a site with particular attributes has 3 years of occurrence vs. 1 or 2.  You will miss out on the mechanism, since a site with persistent occurrence across 3 years is different than 3 separate sites being occupied in a given year.  But, having information across multiple years is still more valuable than a single year.  Everything is an approximation, right?

Hi Nicole,

that's funny, so are you 'donating' your data set to the group ? Anybody meant to take it and write and article on it and perhaps put you in the Acknos ;)

More seriously: better describe your sampling and your questions than just throw the full data set around. So, can you provide info on the following perhaps ? Number of sites (30, OK), number of reps, what protocol (seems distance sampling), how many species detected, 2 years. And, up-front, I don't think you can analyse these data in their full richness in unmarked, but would have to go down the Bayes avenue. In unmarked, there is a new function for modeling of a community based on detection/nondetection data (the model of Rota et al. 2016), but this won't take distance sampling data.

Sollman et al. have described a community version of distance-sampling, for which they provide BUGS code: Sollmann R, Gardner B, Williams KA, Gilbert AT, Veit RR (2016) A hierarchical distance sampling model to estimate abundance and covariate associations of species and communities. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 7(5): 529–537. If you have time, then this seems to me like the basic approach to follow, and then extend that model to two years (which should be fairly easy ---- could do this without or with dynamics).

Best regards --- Marc

 I would say that LCCode has too many levels and perhaps some of them are not present in the data set. regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I've been reading through threads related to this question, but I think this question will address new aspects of the subject.

I'm modeling single-species, single-season occupancy for 15 songbirds.  The process I follow is as follows:

1. run the global model.
2. use mb.gof.test to calculate c-hat.
3. run 10 a priori models of detection probability (occupancy constant).
4. rank detection models with QAIC with c-hat specified (c-hat ranged from 1-3.5 for 12 species to 5.1 - 10 for 3 species).

Before continuing, I have a few question about these steps.   I assumed that since the mb.gof.test is looking at detection history it is appropriate to rank detection models with QAIC by c-hat (when c-hat >1).  On more than 1 occasion, the null model has been the QAIC best detection model.  Is it appropriate to use intercept-only (~1) for detection moving forward to occupancy?

5. run all subsequent occupancy models with detection covariates from the top detection model.
6. run 10 a priori models of occupancy.
7. rank with QAIC with c-hat specified (when c-hat > 1).

When running the global model in order to calculate c-hat, should this be the full model of detection AND occupancy (eg. y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 ~ X4 + X5 + X6), or just the global model of detection?

When c-hat is greater than 4, the models can not be ranked with QAIC because the cut-off is 4; should this species be eliminated from analysis as ability to make inferences will be weak to non-existent any how, or should one  write a custom function to rank by QAIC while allowing c-hat to be > 4 (one of these species was of primary interest [c-hat = 5.1])?

The survey design included 4 visits to 300 points (1 visit was at the very end of the breeding season), and I found that for 2 species where c-hat is > 4, I can reduce this issue by removing the 4th round of surveys and treating it as a 3 visit design.  Is this something that might be frowned upon?
